paragraphs.text: Lesson 25, Agreeing and Disagreeing.
Conversation number one, Agreeing.
Shannon and Kathy are discussing ways to improve the happiness of employees at their company.
Listen to this conversation to learn some phrases for agreeing in English.
I think we need some new policies or programs for motivating our staff.
I couldn't agree more.
We could really use a Boosted Morale.
A lot of our coworkers seem pretty miserable.
Exactly.
It would be great if there was a system of bonuses based on performance.
I suppose so.
But there isn't much extra money in the budget for staff bonuses.
You're right.
Maybe we could allow staff to choose between a monetary bonus and extra vacation time.
Hey, that's a great idea.
I bet the staff members with families would really appreciate that option.
There's no doubt about it.
And I also think we should have more celebrations in the office.
Birthday parties, holiday parties, that sort of thing.
This place is too serious most of the time.
I feel the same way.
Not only would it liven up the office, but it would also help form friendships among the
staff members.
I agree 100%.
Let's write up some of our recommendations and present them to the Vice President.
Conversation Vocabulary and phrases.
Shannon and Kathy are definitely on the same page.
That's an expression meaning they agree or have similar ideas about almost everything.
Here are some phrases for agreeing strongly with someone.
I totally agree with you.
I couldn't agree more.
I agree 100%.
Exactly.
You're absolutely right.
There's no doubt about it.
You can say that again.
Tell me about it.
The last two phrases, you can say that again and tell me about it, are informal phrases.
But all of the phrases I just said can be used when you really want to emphasize how strongly
you agree with the other person.
Now, practice these phrases for expressing ordinary agreement.
I agree.
I share your opinion.
I feel the same way.
You're right.
That's true.
That's for sure.
That's for sure is informal.
Be careful not to make the common mistake of saying, I'm agree.
The correct way to say it is, I agree or I'm in agreement.
Although this second phrase is much more formal.
So it's more common to say simply, I agree.
In the conversation, there's a moment when Kathy agrees that bonuses would be great, but
she is not completely convinced because of the problems with the budget.
Here are some phrases for reluctant agreement when you agree, but you still have some potential
concerns.
I suppose so.
I guess so.
Well, you could be right.
With these phrases, the way you say them and the context of the conversation makes a difference.
Compare these two dialogues.
Sarah's not home.
She must have already left for work.
I guess so.
In this case, I guess so means you're right.
I agree with your idea.
I know you're not happy about moving to a new city, but it will really be better for
our family in the long run.
I guess so.
In this case, I guess so means I agree reluctantly.
I still have some concerns, but I'm not going to argue.
Finally, we have some phrases for partial agreement when you agree with one part of someone's
opinion, but you disagree with another part.
I agree up to a point, but I agree in principle, but say I agree in principle, but when you
agree with an idea, but disagree with the way that idea is applied in practice.
Conversation number two, disagreeing.
Shannon presents a proposal for an expanded employee motivation program to the Vice President
Dan.
Unfortunately, the conversation doesn't go very well.
I respect your opinion, but I see it differently.
The staff should be doing their best work at all times.
They shouldn't need a bunch of extra bonuses and parties.
I agree up to a point.
Of course we should do our best, but making the office environment enjoyable and giving
incentives for good performance will make everyone more likely to do great work.
I'm sorry, but I don't agree.
If someone's not doing their job, they should be fired.
That should be motivation enough for any sensible person.
I understand what you're saying, but I think that we should also have some incentives for
doing great work, not just punishments for poor performance.
I'm of a different opinion.
The company exists to make a profit, not to keep the staff happy.
Actually, I think we can do both.
Happier workers are naturally more dedicated to their work, and that means more profits for
the company.
Well, you could be right, but I'm not willing to make any changes to our policies at this
time.
Okay, but how about a small change?
We could start with just…
I'm sorry, Shannon, but that's my final answer.
You can't be serious.
I can't believe you don't even care about the well-being of your staff.
This is a terrible place to work.
I quit.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
Dan and Shannon don't agree on anything.
This dialogue shows us a number of different ways to disagree politely without disrespecting
or offending the other person.
To disagree politely, you can say, I'm afraid I disagree.
I'm sorry, but I don't agree.
I don't see it that way.
I see it differently.
I'm of a different opinion.
I'm not so sure about that.
Yes, but…
I understand what you're saying, but…
I respect your opinion, but…
You have a right to your opinion, but…
Well, I think…
Actually, I think…
You can see that the first two phrases are the most direct.
The last two phrases are very indirect.
All of these phrases are okay to use in a formal or professional context.
When you want to express strong disagreement, you can use these phrases.
I totally disagree.
I don't agree with that at all.
No way!
That's an informal phrase, and it can be rude.
You can't be serious.
You've got to be kidding.
You're totally wrong, or you're completely wrong.
Many of those phrases are informal and can be rude.
If you want to express strong disagreement in a professional environment, then you should
use only the first two phrases.
I totally disagree.
Or I don't agree with that at all.
With these phrases, only the first two are appropriate for formal or professional situations.
The informal one should only be used among friends, and even then using the might-start
and argument.
By the end of the dialogue, Shannon loses her temper and says, you can't be serious, and
then she quits her job.
Conversation number three, agreeing and disagreeing, short forms.
Now Shannon is looking for a new job.
Her sister Mary is also unemployed, and the two of them are browsing the online job listings
and chatting about their preferences.
I'm going to look for a job at a smaller company.
I don't really enjoy working for big corporations.
Oh, I do.
They offer you a lot of opportunities to advance in your career.
I wouldn't want to work in a dead-end job.
Neither would I, but it would be great to find a company that's still small but growing
fast.
I think it would be exciting.
Me too.
Hey, here's an interesting start-up with a job opening.
Oh, but it's in New York.
I'm not willing to move there.
Well, I am.
A change of scenery would be nice, and I absolutely love New York City.
So do I, but I'd rather visit than live there.
If I get a job there, then you can visit me.
Let's see.
A couple of these organizations are hiring, but I don't really want to work for a non-profit.
Me neither.
The salaries are far too low.
Here are a couple administrative jobs at universities.
I think working at a school would be boring, though.
Really?
I don't.
Maybe I'll apply for some of those positions.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
In this dialogue we see a few examples of ways to agree and disagree using short phrases.
You can use these phrases to agree.
Me too.
Me neither.
So do I.
Neither do I.
So am I.
Neither am I.
So have I.
Neither have I.
So would I.
Neither would I.
Both me too and me neither are used to agree.
The difference is that me too is used to agree with a positive statement, and me neither is
used to agree with a negative statement.
For example, I like my job.
Me too means I also like my job.
I don't like my job.
Me neither.
Means I also don't like my job.
The same rule applies for so and neither use so to agree with positive statements, and
neither to agree with negative statements.
Listen to these examples.
I think this movie is great.
So do I.
I don't think this movie is so good.
Neither do I.
I'm looking forward to the weekend.
So am I.
I'm not looking forward to Monday morning.
Neither am I.
I've always been shy.
So have I.
I've never enjoyed big parties.
Neither have I.
I would love to live abroad.
So would I.
I wouldn't want to work for that company.
Neither would I.
Notice how the word after so or neither matches the one in the original statement.
There are a few times in the conversation where Mary or Shannon disagree with each other's
statements.
I don't really enjoy working for big corporations.
Oh, I do.
I'm not willing to move there.
Well, I am.
I think working at a school would be boring.
Really?
I don't.
When disagreeing in this way, the verb in the response matches the verb in the original
statement, except it reverses from positive to negative or negative to positive to show
the disagreement or difference of opinion.
You can see more examples of this short form and practice using it in the quiz by clicking
the link in the lesson text.
Today's speaking task is to leave a message responding to controversial statements.
Choose five of the ten statements to respond to.
First, say if you agree, disagree, or reluctantly or partially agree, then add one sentence explaining
why.
You can read the list of statements in the lesson text and click on the link to leave your voice
message.
